This photomicrograph of a vaginal smear specimen shows two epithelial cells: one normal cell and another epithelial cell with its surface covered by bacteria, giving it a roughened, stippled appearance known as a clue cell. 2. Clue cells are epithelial cells that have bacteria adhered to their surface, obscuring their borders and imparting a stippled appearance. 3. The presence of clue cells is a diagnostic indicator of bacterial vaginosis. 4. Gardnerella vaginalis, formerly known as Haemophilus vaginalis or Corynebacterium vaginalis, is a Gram-positive bacterium commonly associated with bacterial vaginosis (BV). 5. The vagina is typically colonized by Lactobacillus species, which help regulate the vaginal pH, maintaining it in a low range to inhibit the growth of potentially pathogenic organisms. 6. Gardnerella vaginalis is one such organism that can disrupt the normal vaginal microbiota and is a common cause of bacterial vaginosis. 7. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) and can cause severe reproductive and other health complications if left untreated, including pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. 8. Chlamydia infections are diagnosed using methods such as cell cultures from McCoy cell lines, with identification aided by iodine or fluorescent antibody stains. 9. Inclusion conjunctivitis, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is a type of conjunctival inflammation that can occur in newborns, presenting with redness, eyelid swelling, and pus discharge. 10. Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted disease caused by herpes simplex viruses type 1 (HSV-1) or type 2 (HSV-2), with most cases of genital herpes attributed to HSV-2. 11. Symptoms of genital herpes include one or more blisters on or around the genitals or rectum, which break and leave tender ulcers that may take two to four weeks to heal during the initial outbreak. 12. Recurrent outbreaks of genital herpes are typically less severe and shorter in duration than the initial episode, and the frequency of outbreaks tends to decrease over time. 13. Neonatal herpes, caused by herpes simplex virus, can result in severe complications, including potentially fatal infections in newborns. Cesarean delivery is often performed if active genital herpes is present at the time of delivery. 14. Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is a common sexually transmitted infection that can lead to complications such as disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), which manifests as arthritis, skin lesions, or systemic involvement. 15. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, caused by direct inoculation of Neisseria gonorrhoeae into the conjunctiva, results in inflammation, edema, and purulent discharge from the eye. 16. Untreated gonorrhea can disseminate systemically, causing extra-genital lesions, septic arthritis, or other complications, and is a leading cause of acute septic arthritis in sexually active adults. 17. Diagnosis of gonorrhea involves Gram staining and culture of discharge specimens, with systemic dissemination requiring prompt medical intervention to prevent severe outcomes.
